The Government is deliberately seeking to “divide and dehumanise” people through its migration policy, Labour’s shadow immigration minister has claimed.
Speaking at a fringe event at the Labour conference in Liverpool this morning, Stephen Kinnock said: “My personal opinion is that they see the whole asylum issue as a wedge issue, an opportunity to set communities against each other – to divide, to dehumanise.”
Mr Kinnock said the Government was also using migration to “fire up their base” and “deflect from 13 years of abject failure” across a range of policies, including housing, transport and the economy.
He added: “I think their strategy is backfiring in a very big way because the more they focus public attention on the issue, the more they expose the utter incompetence, neglect and arrogance that they have shown over the last 13 years.”
Shabana Mahmood, the shadow justice secretary, said the Ministry of Justice had been “treated like a carousel ride” by the Tories, with 10 different justice secretaries in 10 years.
“How the Tories have treated this department is beyond a joke,” she told Labour activists as she delivered a speech in the main conference hall this morning.
Ms Mahmood said the nation’s prisons are at “breaking point”.
“The Tories aren’t the party of law and order, they are the party of lawless disorder,” she said, pledging to “rebalance the scales of justice”.
Emily Thornberry told Labour activists in Liverpool that the UK is “trapped in some never ending time loop of Tory incompetence, a groundhog day of gross dereliction”.
But she said that if voters decide to break the cycle and elect a Labour government “we are going to be ready for the task”.

Labour claimed the UK was “still paying the price for the Conservatives’ disastrous mismanagement of the economy” as the party responded to the IMF’s latest economic forecasts (see the post below at 09.52).
Darren Jones, the shadow chief secretary to the Treasury, said: “Britain is still paying the price for the Conservatives’ disastrous mismanagement of the economy that is forecast to leave us with the lowest growth in the G7 and working people worse off.
“Rishi Sunak is too weak to take the tough decisions and Jeremy Hunt has no plan to repair the damage the Conservatives have done to our economy.
“At this week’s party conference in Liverpool, Labour has set out a serious plan to boost growth, make working people better off and get Britain’s future back.”
Britain’s economy will be the worst performing in the G7 next year, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), posing a headache for Rishi Sunak as he fights the next election.
The IMF said higher interest rates were weighing on households and businesses as it downgraded its UK growth forecast from 1pc in 2024 to just 0.6pc.
It warned that UK inflation is expected to remain the highest in the G7 in 2023 and 2024, with Mr Sunak only just on track to meet his goal of halving the headline rate by the end of next year.

Sir Keir Starmer will deliver his Labour Party conference speech at 2pm.
We already have a fairly good idea about what is going to be in there thanks to a fairly extensive overnight trail from Labour.
The main headline is his plan for 10 years in No10, with the leader expected to say Labour will “turn our backs on never-ending Tory decline with a decade of national renewal”.

A Labour government will build a nation where people can be “certain that things will be better for your children”, Sir Keir Starmer will say this afternoon.
Addressing the Labour Party conference in Liverpool, Sir Keir is expected to promise to build a Britain “strong enough, stable enough, secure enough for you to invest your hope, your possibility, your future”.

The tide is turning for Labour in Scotland, Sir Keir Starmer will say this afternoon as he hails the party’s victory in the Rutherglen and Hamilton West by-election last week.

Sir Keir will say that “those days are done” and “we will never go back”. Labour is now a party of “service”, placing the “country first” and the “party second”, he will say.
Labour will fight the next general election on economic growth, Sir Keir Starmer is expected to say today as he attempts to park his tanks firmly on traditionally Tory electoral territory.

Rishi Sunak’s Tory conference speech failed to deliver an opinion poll jump for the Conservatives, a new survey has indicated, in a boost for Sir Keir Starmer as he prepares to deliver his own address in Liverpool today.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/royal-family.title: King Charles has inherited his mother’s ability to steady the ship
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/royal-family.subtitle: Monarch’s speech at Mansion House proves he has knack for saying just enough without descending into sentimentality
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/royal-family.text:
For 70 years, the British public took comfort from the wise words of Queen Elizabeth II.
Not just head of state but grandmother to the nation, just a few carefully chosen thoughts from the late Queen were enough to calm a nation’s nerves through war and conflict, periods of economic and societal strife and even a global pandemic.
Now the task of reigning with reassurance falls to her son and heir, the King, whose Mansion House speech on Wednesday night showed that he has inherited his late mother’s knack for saying just enough without descending into sentimentality or risking accusations of political meddling.
As the longest-serving Prince of Wales in British history, the 74-year-old monarch has already gained a reputation as more outspoken than his predecessor ever was.
Yet this “state of the nation” address was not a “monstrous carbuncle” of a speech but something much more subtle in its architecture.
For amid the grandiose, 18th-century surrounds of the Lord Mayor’s Palladian official residence – most famous for David Lloyd George’s 1911 speech warning the German Empire against opposing British influence during the period leading up to the First World War – came something very much of the moment.
Referring to the “watershed age” that the country is living through, His Majesty said he had been reflecting since his accession last year on what made Britain what it is – an island of shared values, a “community of communities”.
“Every generation lives with its own set of hopes and fears, as if caught in a perpetual tussle between optimism and pessimism, promise and peril,” he said.
Reminding us that “there is far, far more that unites us than divides us,” he spoke of the “deep wells” we can draw upon “to help give ourselves a sense of perspective” and to “see us through good times and bad”.
Royals don’t tend to comment on the so-called culture wars, but there could be no mistaking the monarch’s message as he called for “civility and tolerance” in “our political life and wider national conversation”. He called for us to “think and speak freely”, to listen to each other’s views and disagree “in a way which is passionate but not pugnacious.”
“The words ‘I know my rights’ are wholly familiar – and often true,” he added. “But have we succeeded in equal measure in schooling ourselves, and our communities, in the importance of our responsibilities towards one another?
“Do we pause, instinctively and unerringly, before speaking or acting to ensure we are affording equal weight to both sides of the balance? Our society would be a kinder and gentler place for it.”
It is a question that is gaining increasing relevance since Hamas’s attack on Israel sparked brazenly anti-Semitic protests on the streets of the UK, not to mention an ugly war of words on social media.
While the King did not directly reference what he has already described as the “barbaric acts of terrorism” on Oct 7, his call for the “practice of our religious faiths, in freedom and mutual understanding” did not need much translation.
Nor did his observation that “such understanding, both at home and overseas, is never more vital than at times of international turmoil and heartbreaking loss of life”.
This was an unabashedly “multi-faith” monarch, renewing his Coronation vows.
No speech by Charles III is complete without a reference to our fragile planet, but a little like his son Prince William’s Earthshot Prize, which he will present next month in Singapore, the message was designed to be one of hope, not despair.
Striking a welcome note of optimism in the face of the recent negativity of Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion protests, he championed the “cataract of science, innovation and scholarship which flows into our laboratories and libraries, our lecture halls and our seminar rooms and beyond into our production lines and our knowledge industries” to mitigate against “the biggest battle of all” – global warming and climate change.
While it may be an exaggeration to say that Eeyore has become Tigger, there was undoubtedly something uplifting about the King’s confidence in his subjects being up to the challenges ahead.
At a time when a vocal minority appears intent on rewriting our nation’s history and tearing down its institutions, how refreshing it was to hear a rallying cry for their “labour and loyalty” to be appreciated rather than denigrated.
So too was The Goon Show fan’s reference to the importance of British humour, citing “our ability to laugh at ourselves is one of our great national characteristics”.
“Just as well, given some of the vicissitudes I have faced with frustratingly failing fountain pens this past year!”  he added.
I’m told the King, who writes all his speeches with the help of royal aides, spent recent days “finessing” the final draft with a view to “bringing calm” after what has been a particularly turbulent start, not just to the decade but also the first 12 months of his reign.
For a man often accused of rocking the boat, this latest King’s Speech was a Queen Elizabeth-class lesson in steadying the ship.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/rugby-union/.title: Mud, Sweat and Tears, review: the phoenix from last season's Premiership Rugby ashes
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/rugby-union/.subtitle: It is only the beginning on a very long road to redemption for England’s top tier but the fact that the documentary hits the mark is a start
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/rugby-union/.text:
In the list of potential targets for a sporting documentary, the semi-finals and final of last season’s Gallagher Premiership – a season in which three clubs went to the wall and English rugby’s showpiece was interrupted by Just Stop Oil protestors at Twickenham – would probably not be the most desirable of starting points. Not, at least, if the aim is to focus on the league’s strengths ahead of the launch of a new season on Friday night. Talk about beating against the tide; about polishing the proverbial.
And yet, out of the ashes of last season, Premiership Rugby and Prime Video have delivered a phoenix. It is only the beginning on a very long road to recovery and redemption for England’s top tier, but the fact that the documentary hits the mark is a start.
The two-part series, which will debut on Prime Video this Thursday, shadows the four Premiership semi-finalists - Saracens, Sale, Leicester and Northampton – ahead of each of their respective knock-out matches, before honing in on the two finalists. There is heart-ache, there is levity and there is motivation; as well as some fascinating – and uncensored –  glimpses behind the curtain of the Premiership’s elite.
Characters are a motif. At Saracens, the stories of stalwart Jackson Wray, schoolboy hotshot Ben Earl and the injured Elliot Daly are told; similarly at Sale, where the spotlight shines on director of rugby Alex Sanderson, superstar George Ford and tyro Gus Warr. Kitmen are given prominence and at Northampton, too, fly-half Finn Smith is tasked with explaining the machinations of the sport for those who might be new to it.
Of the directors of rugby and head coaches featured, Northampton’s Phil Dowson is the unabated star. Mark McCall, palpably one of the game’s pre-eminent minds, is too diffident to shine; Richard Wigglesworth, as interim Leicester head coach, is not given as much prominence with his imminent departure to England on the horizon; and Sanderson brings lovable, northern heart and soul but occasionally tips over into the Brentian. “Let’s enjoy it, not endure it,” he says ahead of his team’s preparation for the final; his heart could not be more in the right place but it is a soundbite which would be just as at home in the offices of Slough’s Wernham Hogg as at Sale’s Carrington training base.
Among the quartet, it is Dowson’s charisma that is most unexpected. The former flanker, with the lowest profile of the four, is understated; the fierce leader of Northampton’s underdogs. The erstwhile impression of the Saints’ director of rugby might have been one of a loyal, thinking rugby man, but not necessarily someone with the bravado to talk his players out of the trenches. With Lewis Ludlam in tow – the documentary’s other undoubted phenom – one might have been ready to boot up and take a spot on the Saints’ bench.
“People don’t rate our chances in this game because they don’t know our narrative, our story,” Dowson dictates ahead of Northampton’s semi-final against Saracens. “Generally people don’t give a f--- about people that come third or fourth or second.
“All of these players here [on the screen] have come through the academy - home-grown. It’s absolutely integral to cohesion. Players growing up together, playing code together, going through life together - that’s f---ing powerful lads. People don’t have any clue, they go: ‘Northampton are ok.’ They don’t know the frustration that sits in this room, the f---ing endless work we’ve put in... They don’t know that because they haven’t seen it. We want to go beyond, do more. That’s our narrative.”
It is a shame that it was in vain.
As well as characters, the wider landscape of English rugby, while not dwelt on, is acknowledged. This documentary is not some tin-eared PR fantasy, taking place in a world where the Saracens salary-cap scandal did not exist; where Leicester’s coaching team was not plundered by the Rugby Football Union last season; and where Worcester Warriors, Wasps and London Irish all feature in a 13-team league. There is authenticity and honesty.
The league and the producers’ willingness to paint as authentic a picture as possible of the play-offs has paid off, but it means that any hint of artificiality is easily discernible. One of few criticisms is the decision to ask the league’s two leading commentators, Nick Mullins and Ali Eykyn, to retrospectively re-record snippets of commentary to play over the documentary’s match footage. It is slightly muffled, too, as if to give the impression that the commentary is genuine, but the result is something out of Ted Lasso or the Fifa video games.
Amid the gravitas, there are welcome moments of levity, the brightest of which comes courtesy of Navdeep Singh Sandhu, Sale’s physiotherapist, who jokes to Manu Tuilagi that he touches the centre’s body more than his wife’s, leaving the England international in hysterics.
The mini-series reaches an emotional crescendo with Sanderson’s pre-match speech to his Sale charges which, like Dowson earlier, comes in vain. Sanderson reveals that his sister-in-law died a fortnight before the final - with the funeral in the build-up week - that his mother is in remission from cancer and three weeks previously his father suffered a heart attack, meaning he can only be at the final in a wheelchair.
“It makes you reflect,” Sanderson says poignantly. The Sharks’ director of rugby is a noble leader, a man of integrity and it would be fascinating to hear his thoughts on that week, and the maelstrom of emotions, four months on.
“Fairy-tales don’t come f---ing true, boys - life’s taught me that over the past few weeks,” he adds, regarding Saracens’ desire to bounce back swiftly and win the title after their salary-cap scandal. Little did he know that he was foreshadowing his own team’s fate.
The Premiership, however, after last season’s nadir, will be hoping that the words of Sale’s director of rugby eventually ring true, that there is a fairy-tale on the horizon. This is as good a start as any.
Mud, Sweat and Tears: Premiership Rugby available now on Prime Video

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/columnists/2.title: Walking faster will do wonders for your health – and everyone else’s sanity
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/columnists/2.subtitle: A recent study extols the benefits of striding around quickly, something many Londoners will be all too pleased about
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/columnists/2.text:
According to a new scientific study, people who walk quickly live longer than those who walk slowly. They’re also vastly less likely to die of cancer or heart disease.
Personally, I’m delighted to hear it. And so, I suspect, is everyone else who has ever worked in London. This is because slow-walking tourists are the absolute bane of our lives.
No matter where you happen to be in London, you can immediately tell the difference between the office workers and the tourists. The office workers are the ones storming along the pavement at 400mph in a furious frenzy of self-importance. The tourists, meanwhile, are the ones bumbling about in an oblivious trance, getting in everyone else’s way.
I for one have long argued that London’s busy pavements should be divided into lanes, like motorways, to stop the tourists and the office workers constantly crashing into each other. In my view, it’s a serious indictment of Sadiq Khan that after seven years as Mayor he has still yet to implement such an urgently needed scheme.
But perhaps, thanks to this excellent new study by the University of Leicester, my scheme will no longer be necessary. Having learnt of the dangers of dawdling, tourists will finally pick up the pace, and walk at the same speed as the rest of us. And if they don’t, we can always remind them. Very politely, of course. After all, we only have their best interests at heart.
Indeed, we always have. Back in the late Noughties, it was widely reported that more than a million people had joined a Facebook group entitled ‘I Want to Punch Slow-Walking People in the Back of the Head’. At the time, some observers considered the name of this group to be horribly callous. In retrospect, though, we can now see that it was anything but. The members of the group were merely anxious to help tourists avoid contracting heart disease, that was all. Obviously a punch in the back of the head would have been a touch excessive. But a little tap on the tourist’s shoulder, along with some gentle encouragement to get a move on and stop blocking the street like a backpack-wearing bollard, might have saved goodness knows how many tourists’ lives.
From now on, happily, the Facebook group’s members will be able to rest easy. Tourists, though, won’t be the only beneficiaries of this wonderful study. Because, the next time the nitwits of Just Stop Oil clog up the roads with one of their “slow walking” protests, the police will be legitimately entitled to break it up – for the sake of the nitwits’ own health.
To be frank, I’ve always felt that such protests could endanger these activists’ health anyway – given the risk that, at any moment, an enraged driver might erupt from their car and start walloping them over the head with a wrench. Now that science has confirmed that walking slowly carries numerous other health hazards, however, the activists will surely see sense and pack it in.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/10.title: Greta Thunberg could be allowed to return to UK despite protest arrest
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/10.subtitle: If the activist is charged with an offence it is thought it would not carry a sanction serious enough to warrant a UK ban
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/10.text:
Greta Thunberg will be allowed to return to the UK despite being arrested at an environmental protest in London.
The 20-year-old Swedish activist, wearing a badge with the slogan “Oily Money Out,” was placed into a police van after officers led her away from the InterContinental Hotel on Park Lane, where a meeting of oil executives was being held.
She stood calmly as police officers spoke to her, while protesters could be heard shouting “thank you Greta” as she looked out and smiled from the vehicle.
If Ms Thunberg is charged with an offence, which she has not yet been, it would not carry a sanction serious enough to warrant her being automatically banned from the UK.
Guidelines state that the automatic deportation of foreign criminals under the UK Borders Act 2007 only allows the deportation of those who have committed serious criminal offences requiring a term of imprisonment of 12 months or more.
While it is not yet clear what Ms Thunberg has been arrested for, charges under section 14 of the Public Order Act, which many protesters at the event were arrested for, are usually dealt with by way of a fine.
Organised by the group Fossil Free London, demonstrators attempted to block access to the venue by sitting and standing on the pavement by the entrance.
They also unfurled a banner on the side of the building.
Oil industry executives had gathered there for the annual Energy Intelligence Forum, with speakers including the heads of Saudi Arabia’s Aramco and Norway’s Equinor as well as  Graham Stuart, the Net Zero Minister.
The protesters say that fossil fuel companies are deliberately slowing the global energy transition to renewables in order to make more profit, highlighting how this year’s UN climate conference president Sultan al Jaber is also the chief executive of oil company Abu Dhabi National Oil Co.
Before her arrest, Ms Thunberg addressed journalists outside the hotel, saying: “The world is drowning in fossil fuels. Our hopes and dreams and lives are being washed away by a flood of greenwashing and lies.
“It has been clear for decades that the fossil fuel industries were well aware of the consequences of their business models, and yet, they have done nothing.
“The opposite – they have actively delayed, distracted and denied the causes of the climate crisis and spread doubts about their own engagement in it.”
Last week, Ms Thunberg was ordered by a court in Malmo to pay a 2,250 kroner (£170) fine for disobeying police during a protest at an oil terminal in the city on July 24.
She joined activists in London where demonstrations are expected to run throughout the three-day meeting of oil executives.
Activists from Greenpeace abseiled down from the roof of the hotel to unfurl a banner reading “make big oil pay”, while a strong wind billowed the message and the protesters against the side of the building.
Others held banners and pink umbrellas with eyes painted on at both ends of Hamilton Place, stifling access to the hotel.
They shouted “oily money out” and “cancel the conference”, while others lit yellow and pink smoke flares.
A white fence surrounded the hotel entrance keeping protesters out while police smuggled conference attendees through the crowd of chanting activists and a samba band.
However, protesters were successful in disrupting the programme of events, with Shell chief executive Wael Sawan revealing he would deliver his speech remotely as he could not access the hotel.
The chief executives of trading houses Gunvor and Trafigura missed their appearances at the conference because they were stuck outside, according to Bloomberg News.
Police confirmed they had made 21 arrests by the afternoon, with one arrested on suspicion of criminal damage.
A statement from the Metropolitan Police said that officers imposed conditions on the protesters under the Public Order Act at 12.32pm.
The statement added: “Officers asked the protesters to move from the road onto the pavement, which would enable them to continue with their demonstration without breaching the conditions.
“A number of protesters failed to do so and we have now made a further 14 arrests for section 14 of the Public Order Act and a further one for criminal damage. Officers remain on the scene.”

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/10.title: Watch: Met Police take 40 minutes to remove Just Stop Oil activists from Parliament Square
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/10.subtitle: Protesters blocked traffic by ‘slow marching’ across all three carriageways before 62 were arrested
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/10.text:
Police took around 40 minutes to tackle dozens of Just Stop Oil activists off the road in central London, despite outnumbering them.
Around 65 activists from the eco-group “slow marched” across all three carriageways around Parliament Square at 10am on Monday, causing traffic gridlock.
The Metropolitan Police appeared to have been caught off guard, calling for reinforcements while activists continued with the slow marching – walking at a snail’s pace – until forcibly removed.
Despite vowing to crack down with swift arrests under the Public Order Act, the Met’s 80 officers and 20 police vehicles took 40 minutes to remove them all.
In a statement, Scotland Yard said it had made 62 arrests under section seven of the Act, meaning “interference with use or operation of key national infrastructure”, and had “arrived four minutes after receiving the initial report”.
Tensions flared at times, with a van driver and a coach barging past the Just Stop Oil road blockade, while a taxi driver told the protesters: “You’re disgusting, all of you – my passengers have got a train to catch.”
The taxi driver told the Telegraph: “Not only have we had the Palestinian march at the weekend causing havoc, now we’ve got this – costing people money – and I’ve got a police officer taking photos of my cab like I’m in the wrong.”
Some passers-by applauded Just Stop Oil, but another onlooker shouted: “Get a job and have a wash. Because you’re all rich you don’t have to work – but these people do, you know.”
Eventually, police took to ripping the group’s orange banners away and admonishing the activists for “obstructing us further” by lying down on the pavement after being placed in handcuffs. One protester told them: “It was safe until the police arrived.”
Several elderly women were seen being carried into police vans by officers as they refused to comply.
Groups of foreign tourists on guided tours of Westminster watched as the protesters, wearing hi-vis clothing, sprawled across the pavement and carriageway.
A Met spokesman said the operation took 40 minutes because that was how long it took to get the large number of protesters into police vans.
Scotland Yard commander Kyle Gordon said: “This is an extremely busy time for officers across London who are providing reassurance to communities following the escalation of the conflict between Israel and Hamas.
“It’s unacceptable that we are having to remove officers, who are carrying out vital work in their communities at a time where there is a large number of hate crime being reported to us, to police Just Stop Oil.
“We recognise that many people are fed up with disruptive protests but we also have a duty to make sure anyone who wants to protest lawfully can do so.”
Just Stop Oil is resuming daily slow marches in London from this week. The group, which is demanding that the Government scraps all new oil and gas licences, has vowed to continue “until we win”.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/10.title: The strange story of a polar bear, a farm in Suffolk and Jamie Oliver’s best friend
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/10.subtitle: It would be easy to be cynical about polar bears in Suffolk – but Jimmy Doherty believes wildlife parks have a role to play in conservation
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/10.text:
Picture the largest polar bear reserve in Europe.
It is not in the northernmost reaches of Finland or the snowy Alps but, in fact, in Suffolk – the surprising pet project of farmer and television presenter Jimmy Doherty, best known for the BBC series Jimmy’s Farm, and for presenting various other series with Jamie Oliver, his childhood friend.
A polar bear in flat, green Suffolk, with the mainline train to London Liverpool Street rumbling along the horizon every half hour or so, is an incongruous sight. It’s hardly the Arctic tundra.
But polar bears were never part of Doherty’s plan. This was a rescue mission.
A year and a half ago, Doherty, 48, received a call to say a wildlife park – Orsa Rovdjurspark (Predator Park) in central Sweden – was closing down. It had been sold to developers and the animals needed to be rehomed by a certain date or they would be put down.
“Amongst those animals was a group of polar bears – among them, Ewa, a female who was 18 years old… it was very unlikely she could be rehomed,” he says. “I never wanted those conventional animals you see [in zoos], like tigers, or polar bears. But here I am.”
On the edge of his eponymous farm and wildlife park, which is already home to paddocks of sheep, cows, goats, capybaras, tapirs and camels and more than 90 other species, there is a high fence.
Concealed from public view (until later this month) sits a newly built 16-acre enclosure with deep springs and woodland, confirmed by the European Association of Zoos and Aquaria (Eaza) to be Europe’s largest. Sat in the middle of her new home is Ewa, face turned to the sky, sniffing the air.
So far, Doherty has discovered that Ewa’s favourite food is honey and she particularly likes rolling in bark chippings, but he isn’t trying to pretend polar bears are cute and cuddly.
“She likes a bit of love, but you can never forget that this is a wild animal and the planet’s largest [land] predator,” he says.
Doherty, with his reputation for rescuing exotic species as varied as racoons and macaques, got the call as a last-ditch attempt to save Ewa. Initially, he says, he was “terrified” of rehoming the world’s largest land-based carnivore in an enclosure – albeit a very large one – just two miles from the suburbs of Ipswich.
His wife, Michaela “thought we were crazy,” he says. They have four daughters and live nearby. “She had nightmares… [she] envisioned the idea of waking up and there being a polar bear in the garden. That’s what you think, isn’t it. What if it gets out?”
But he couldn’t bear the thought of Ewa being put down. “That was the main thing. But out of that, we didn’t just want an enclosure with a polar bear, it had to tell a bigger story. That’s why we rehomed the Arctic wolves – we’re telling the story of the tundra,” he says.
“I’ve always thought if you can do something, you should do something, rather than going, that’s too much work, I can’t be bothered.”
Ewa’s 1,000-mile journey from Orsa with a specialist courier took her through Sweden by road, to Germany by ferry, and then to England via Le Shuttle [Eurotunnel] to Folkestone.
But when she arrived, tragedy struck. Doherty had planned to rehome her two-year-old cub, Miki, with her, but she died in transit, fuelling a small group of vocal “naysayers” (as Doherty calls them) who have argued that rehoming the bears in Suffolk is unwise.
“We did an autopsy pretty much immediately, three vets have verified it… unfortunately unbeknownst to us, she had an enlarged heart and could have died at any moment,” he says. “You just want to pull your hair out… but it’s one of those things.”
We are here to discuss polar bears, but there is an elephant in the room. Is it sensible, or indeed responsible, to have a polar bear best suited to an icy environment in Suffolk, where average temperatures are 20C-23C in summer?
On this point, Doherty is well prepared. “From afar, it’s easy to [cast] aspersions. But when you look at the details, you understand this bear has no other option,” he says. Ewa has lived her entire life in a wildlife park – if she were released into the wild, says Doherty, she wouldn’t last long as she would likely be killed by a rival and has no hunting skills.
Several experts were consulted on the viability of keeping polar bears in Suffolk’s temperate climate. “In 2018, in Churchill, Manitoba, the polar bear capital of the world, it was 31C. Polar bears aren’t always on the ice,” says Douglas Richardson, the zoological consultant who alerted Doherty to the closure of Predator Park.
“I’ve worked with polar bears in zoos all over the world and I’ve seen them out on hot days. This idea that they can’t cope with a warmer climate [is incorrect]. They cope very well – it’s not a problem.”
The Highland Wildlife park has successfully housed polar bears since 2009. “We [also] looked at Yorkshire Wildlife Park – they have polar bears and their temperature range is very similar to ours,” says Doherty.
“We probably have more sunlight hours than they do, and they probably have a bit more rain. But average summer temperatures were one degree different. We looked at Hudson Bay, Canada, where you find them in the wild, and summer temperatures are 25C.
“We’re fairly confident we can provide a home that’s agreeable – it’s not like where you see polar bears in Mexico Zoo or Singapore Zoo. So long as we give them the areas where they can regulate their temperature and cool themselves down, they’re absolutely fine.” Ultimately, for Ewa, it is better than the alternative: “I can live with that because I know the bear hasn’t been shot.”
It would be easy to be cynical about the fact that Ewa will be a visitor attraction, but underpinning this mission is Doherty’s long-held belief that modern wildlife parks and zoos have an important role to play in the conservation of endangered species – a belief that is now officially recognised.
In a “position statement” released earlier this month, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) said it “proudly recognizes and applauds the significant contributions made by botanic gardens, aquariums, and zoos in their critical mission of conserving wild animals.”
Doherty doesn’t call Jimmy’s Farm a zoo – “We’re a wildlife park, because we have a lot of space, and we don’t have so many animals,” he says – but he is broadly in favour of them. “I think people have got to look at the conservation [work] zoos do, and the access they provide to amazing species that are so inspirational.”
Tundras are among the world’s harshest and least hospitable areas, characterised by low temperatures and little rainfall, and they are under threat as the permafrost melts as a result of rising temperatures.
“Everyone talks about the rainforest disappearing, and the loss of biodiversity… but there is a huge environment that spans North America all the way across the top of Eurasia – the tundra – that is disappearing so quickly because of climate change.”
The first arrival to the new exhibit, named The Lost Lands of the Tundra, was a pack of 13 Arctic wolves rehomed from Cumbria Wildlife Park last month. They needed to be kept a secret from visitors and dog walkers on the nearby footpath while they settled in. “A lot guessed… but some people said giraffes,” says Doherty.
Some passing train passengers assumed they were an unusual breed of sheep, he says. He didn’t correct them. The wolves will be joined in the park by Arctic foxes and the farm’s resident herd of reindeer, as well as more polar bears “by the end of this year or the beginning of next year”.
Word has got out. As we make our way across the park, a regular visitor with a buggy exclaims: “Polar bears! Really? I thought that was just a drunken story.”
The reserve – which has cost £800,000 so far – stretches out below us from what will be the public viewing area. It has been well thought out, with multiple “homes” and hiding places for Ewa and whichever bears end up joining her, plus six acres of woodland with “lots of deadfall and trees [Ewa] can break up and sniff around… and smell the squirrels and the bluebells.”
It has been designed with high and low areas, which is “not only about the sight, it’s all about the olfactory stimulus… all the smells coming in”.
It also contains two coldwater springs, one 14 metres deep and one 8 metres deep, which is important for the bear’s temperature regulation. There is a secure bark enclosure and a saltwater bath (“like a spa,” says Doherty) and three interconnected areas through which the different animals can roam.
He plans to introduce a “carbon classroom” to “explain the things we can all do to help mitigate climate change… I don’t mean glue yourself to walls and placards and stuff,” he adds, referring to climate activist groups Extinction Rebellion and Just Stop Oil. “Just simple stuff, like turning the lights off, and what we do about food waste.”
Doherty studied zoology and was working on a PHD in entomology when he decided to try his hand at farming rare pig breeds in Suffolk. He moved to Wherstead, Ipswich, as a 24-year-old and set up the The Essex Pig Company on the site of Jimmy’s Farm, which is now home to the wildlife park, a restaurant and farm shop.
It is a challenging time for British farmers, he says – the sector is in “flux” with the pressures of rising costs, climate change, and the shift in agricultural policy post-Brexit. “I’m bored of people creating models and pontificating and never getting a bit of dirt under their fingernails,” he says.
“I hate the idea of someone saying farming… is destroying the world. I’m like, ‘Are you an idiot?’ We all eat three times a day. The idea that a plant-based diet is going to save the world is, for me, complete nonsense. We forget that it’s an urban elite luxury to be plant-based. I’d much rather focus on local, mixed farming.”
And bears, of course. The next step is to rehome a European brown bear, Diego, who Doherty visited in Sweden, “before it’s too late. That’s a complicated one because we need to move him before he goes into hibernation, and we’ve got to find somewhere to put him so he can sleep through the winter,” he says.
“My wife said: ‘No more bears! We’ve got no money left. You’ve just taken a massive loan out,’” says Doherty. “But it’s like going into any animal sanctuary and there’s that one dog left waiting for adoption that seems to say, ‘What about me?’” He couldn’t resist.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/10.title: Just Stop Oil protesters throw paint over Natural History Museum dinosaur
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/10.subtitle: Two men dressed in medical scrubs threw powder towards the replica skeleton as visitors attended Titanosaur exhibition
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/10.text:
Just Stop Oil protesters have thrown orange powder on the huge replica dinosaur the forms the centrepiece of the Natural History Museum.
The Titanosaur: Life as the Biggest Dinosaur exhibition was closed to the public on Thursday after the men, both medics, staged a protest beneath a 121ft replica skeleton.
Visitors watched on as Dr Will Stableforth, a consultant gastroenterologist, and Steve Fay, a physiotherapist, covered the gigantic model in orange cornstarch.
The replica is on loan from the Museo Paleontológico Egidio Feruglio (MEF) in Argentina and was made using fossils unearthed from South America in 2014.
The men immediately knelt on the museum floor and displayed a banner that read: “For health’s sake Just Stop Oil.”
Police officers arrested two people on suspicion of criminal damage. They remain in custody.
Museum staff said the exhibition had been temporarily closed on Thursday as the gallery was inspected for any potential damage.
A spokesperson from the museum said: “We are aware of a Just Stop Oil protest which took place at the Natural History Museum this afternoon.
“The police have been informed and the affected gallery has been temporarily closed to visitors.
“If you have tickets booked for the Titanosaur exhibition this afternoon, you will be refunded. Please contact feedback@nhm.ac.uk.”
Speaking before the action, Dr Stableforth, from Truro, Cornwall, said: “As an NHS medical consultant I’ve spent many years looking after patients with diseases which, at their root, are caused by fossil fuels.
“I have done everything legal I can to get our message across. Most of that has been ineffective; so it’s time to break the law. I cannot see another way at this time.
“The climate crisis is a healthcare emergency for every single one of us. We demand an end to any new fossil fuels and immediate climate action prioritising public health rather than big business.”
Mr Fay, from the Hebrides, added: “Like this long-extinct dinosaur, we are in grave danger of following in its footsteps.
“We know we are in a climate emergency with breakdowns in weather patterns and deaths of millions on the near horizon, yet our government pursues ever greater exploitation of oil and gas reserves.”
A Metropolitan Police spokesperson said: “Two people have been arrested on suspicion of criminal damage at the Natural History Museum. Two activists from Just Stop Oil vandalised one of the exhibits with orange paint.”

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/10.subtitle: Climate group preparing for thousands of its members to be detained as it abandons previous strategy of leaving the road when ordered
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/10.text:
Just Stop Oil protesters have vowed to slow march until police arrest them, in an escalation of disruption that is set to take place next week.
The eco-activist group is beginning a new round of slow marches on London’s streets from Monday that are expected to bring traffic to a standstill.
The “unprecedented” daily roadblocks would continue “week after week until we win”, the group said of its demand that the Government grants no more new oil or gas licences.
But in a ramping up of tensions, The Telegraph can reveal that Just Stop Oil is preparing for “thousands of arrests” by abandoning its previous strategy of leaving the road when ordered, to instead carry on regardless.
A spokesman told The Telegraph: “It’s looking good – we have record levels of sign-ups, much bigger than previously. We’re probably looking at thousands of arrests.
“Previously, our supporters were not aiming to be arrested, but now they’re saying ‘we’re going to carry on slow marching when the police tell us to leave the road’, so that’s the difference this time around.
“Section 12 has always been part of the Public Order Act and in our previous slow marches, people were not willing to be arrested so they would comply with the police’s conditions on legal protest.
“But this is a change of tactics now, meaning this time around it’s liable to be a bit more disruptive – people will not get off the road when asked, so police will be forced to remove them.”
Just Stop Oil deployed the slow march tactic – in which activists walk at a snail’s pace along a busy road, blocking all traffic – earlier this year after noticing it exploited a legal loophole that meant they evaded arrest.
Following public outcry and pressure from ministers, the Met Police started issuing orders under Section 12 of the Public Order Act for them to leave the road or be arrested for causing serious disruption.
Scotland Yard has issued an open letter to Just Stop Oil to halt “their stated intention to cause maximum indiscriminate disruption”, but the group replied by telling the police to prosecute “acts of genocide” against the climate.
The co-founders of Just Stop Oil, Roger Hallam, 57, and 29-year-old Indigo Rumbelow, were arrested in dawn raids earlier this month in which officers “confiscated papers”.
But the group is refusing to relent, with more high-profile events including live BBC shows now in their sights.
Asked about reports they could run onto the dance floor on Strictly Come Dancing, a spokesman said: “We will do anything, because everything we know and love is under threat so we don’t rule out disrupting sporting or cultural events including Strictly Come Dancing.”
